meta.title: Is the Judge the Bottleneck?
meta.subtitle: A controlled GA vs NSGA-II study of LLM-guided haiku and limerick generation
meta.author: Sakthi C R
meta.affil: M.Tech Artificial Intelligence, Amrita School of Computing, Coimbatore
meta.guide: Guide: Dr. Bagavathi C., Assistant Professor (Sr. Gd.), Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham

summary: Twelve experiments pit a plain genetic algorithm against NSGA-II inside the same language-model poetry pipeline, with the generator, the judge, the fitness terms and the budget held identical.
The two algorithms finish in a dead heat: mean fitness 0.8368 against 0.8358, a gap of 0.0010.

Auditing the fitness function explains why — the language model used as a judge changes its own score on 74% of poems when it reads them again, which is about twenty times larger than the effect being measured.

findings.s: GA 0.8368 vs NSGA-II 0.8358 over 12 runs. Wins split 3-2 with one tie; Wilcoxon p = 1.0.

findings.l: of poems scored differently on a re-read
findings.s: 39 of 53 poems changed score when the same judge read them again with the same prompt.
One judge reading carries half the weight of F, so its instability swamps the algorithmic difference.

judge.note: 53 poems, each scored 3 times by one judge on one shared rubric.
tests: Published human beats deliberately bad: p = 0.005 (haiku), p = 0.001 (limerick). The judge does discriminate.

Evolved beats published human limericks: p = 0.0005, every one of the six above all fifteen. But coherence is identical (4.72 vs 4.73) — the whole gap is imagery, literary devices and originality. The rubric has no dimension for humour, which is what a Lear limerick is built on.

setup.stop: stop early if best F improves < 0.01 for 2 generations
setup.runs: one run per cell, 283 candidates evaluated in total

limits: One run per cell, so per-cell differences cannot be separated from run-to-run variation.
Noise was measured with the 4-dimension calibration rubric, not the 5-dimension production rubric.
One judge model and one provider; order and self-preference biases are not controlled.
The only human signal is a single accept/reject per run, by the author, who was not blind to the condition.
A tokeniser defect mis-counted syllables in words with a typographic apostrophe; two final poems are re-scored offline here, but the effect inside the search cannot be undone.
